speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in order that there may be a definite understanding of the position which the government takes, I would like to make it clear that it is not regarded as being in the public interest that any departmental correspondence which takes place between the engineers at the capital and the divisional engineers at Quebec, Edmonton or Victoria with respect to the possible expenditure of public moneys, should be brought down until such intention has crystallized into action. Non constat no action may ever be taken. My hon. friend now suggests the deletion of the word "estimates" but this motion covers correspondence between officials of the department and the department and plans and specifications which may never result in anything being done, and to suggest that they should be brought down in this house is something which I think has not heretofore been done. The minute public moneys are voted, whether or not they are expended, the minute any action is taken which indicates a crystallization of the intention into action, the minute estimates are passed which indicate contemplated action, then any government would say that such documents should be brought down. My hon. friend has thirty-eight motions on the order paper, and I ask him: Will you say that work has begun within any locality mentioned in these motions, or that an appropriation appears in the estimates for this year or appeared in the estimates of last year with respect to them? If the hon. gentleman can answer that question in the affirmative, then we will pass the motion to bring down the papers at once. I think my hon. friend on reflection will realize that this is the practice which heretofore has been established and must be followed if the government is to be carried on at all with any degree of regard to business considerations.
Let me put this case' to my right hon. friend. A number of persons write letters to the Prime Minister with respect to public works, and these he forwards to the minister. The minister sends his engineer down to report upon the matter. Reports are made, of which the Prime Minister is not aware. In reality, the writing of the letters and securing the reports, et cetera, formed part of a general plan whereby it was hoped to secure the expenditure of public moneys for a particular project. A file is made. This is brought down in the house and hon. gentlemen promoting the project say:	"Behold! Look
what we have been doing all the time to promote the interests of our constituencies. There was never any likelihood of the government doing anything in the matter, it is

true, but look what we have done." Now, if the hon. gentleman will say, with respect to any one of these motions standing in his name, that any public money has been voted or an estimate submitted for the expenditure of public moneys, we will pass the motion at once. Otherwise, the whole basis on which business is to be transacted is gone.

In none of these cases,
I believe, were there any estimates or was an3' money appropriated either last year or the year before. The case is as I have stated it before. May I ask the leader of the government whether it would be possible for me to inspect all these various records myself. That would expedite matters and would cause the government no inconvenience. As the member representing the county, I submit that I am entitled to see these records.

I wish briefly to associate myself with what the last speaker has said. The other day I made a motion similar to this, [DOT]with the idea of finding out why the government had not taken action. So far as I know, the government did not come to a

speechtext:
I promised yesterday, in response to
a question asked by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth), to get some information as to the treatment of certain prisoners in the preferred class penitentiary near Kingston. The matter arises out of a somewhat lurid article which appeared in the Toronto Globe of the 8th day of June, referring to those prisoners. I have received the following information from the superintendent of penitentiaries and I shall give it to the house just as I have received it:
There are ten former Toronto brokers confined in the preferred class penitentiary. Superintendent has seen .all of these men at work at times. He has personally interviewed each one of them. He has seen them employed on cement mixers, digging ditches, assisting in installing an intake pipe for water system, building a stone wall, painting buildings, building two pump-houses, farming, gardening, unloading material at railway siding, cataloguing library books, .assisting .in the checking of stores, and storing of goods as received, several employed at carpenter work, washing and repairing inmates' clothing, assisting the accountant, the storekeeper, the engineer. One of the oldest inmates is steadily employed as a clerk in the deputy warden's office. They are treated in exactly similar manner to all the other inmates. One is employed part time in the hospital and part time at other work. In fact, they are employed wherever their abilities can be utilized.
There are 200 inmates at the preferred class institution. These men are all short-timers and selected because they are short-timers whose offences have not been brutal or vicious, and, whose employment under existing conditions is considered safe. There are no walls and only a wire fence around the dormitories where they sleep.
A philanthropic gentleman, no friend of the ex-brokers, presented the institution with a gramophone and a number of records. This has been the only music provided in the institution.
A nucleus of a library of carefully selected books has been secured. It is the intention that this will be added to another year.
This is all in conformity with the discussion which took place in the house when the vote for a preferred class penitentiary was being passed. This is not an ordinary penitentiary, but one for the purpose of giving men an opportunity to reform. It is for short-time men, the definition of that being a sentence up to four years, for first offenders

speechtext: The house resumed from Tuesday, June 9, consideration of the motion of the Right Hon. R. B. Bennett (Minister of Finance) that Mr. Speaker do not now leave the chair for the house to go into committee of ways and means, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Ralston.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, let me at the outset congratulate most heartily the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) on his able review of the finances [DOT]of the country. No more comprehensive and masterly statement giving such elaborate and detailed information as to the national finances, our trade and commerce, the estimated receipts and estimated expenditures, and the ways and means of raising supply lias ever before been presented to this house. It is a budget in the truest sense and significance of the term.
We in the province of New Brunswick are naturally proud of the right hon. gentleman who now occupies the high and enviable position of Prime Minister of this fair dominion, and there are none who rejoice more over his success than those of us in the county of Northumberland, which constituency I have the honour to represent in this parliament. It was there the right hon. gentleman laid the foundations of his career, a career which has now culminated in his occupying the highest position in the gift of his fellow citizens, and it is only natural that those in the county of Northumberland should rejoice heartily at the success he has achieved.
This budget, Mr. Speaker, is of particular moment to those of us from the maritime provinces, because we realize that we have received the greatest concession for our coal industry that has been granted to us since the days of Sir John A. Macdonald. The increase in the tariff on anthracite coal to 40 cents and on bituminous coal to 75 cents enables the great coal industry of the maritime provinces, particularly that of Nova Scotia, to compete more successfully in the Canadian market. Tha-t industry has the added advantage of the subventions which this government has decided upon, and I say (Mr. Bennett.]
that the concessions which have been given to the coal industry, not only of Nova Scotia but of New Brunswick-because in the latter province we are interested, although to a smaller extent, in coal mining-reflect very creditably indeed upon this administration.
For a number of years, Mr. Speaker, practically a solid bloc from Nova Scotia supported hon. gentlemen opposite. What did the maritime provinces-the province of Nova Scotia and the province of New Brunswick- receive from my hon. friends opposite? What did they receive from the King government, in the way of encouraging the great coal industry employing in the neighbourhood of 13,000 men out of a total of some 30,000 men engaged in this great industry throughout the Dominion? I submit that the concessions already given are a step in the right direction, and I hope there will be further concessions when the time is opportune. This is one of our basic industries, and I respectfully submit it should be given as much consideration, say, as the automobile industry, for I am told that there are double the number of men employed in the coal industry in comparison with those engaged in the manufacture of automobiles and automobile parts.
Coming to the question of unemployment, we must admit that unemployment is a world-wide condition, but statistics go to show that in this respect we are immeasurably better off in the dominion than they are in the mother country or in the United States.

speechtext:
The people of Canada, I may tell my right hon. friend, spoke the truth when they spoke last July. Unemployment started under the regime of my hon. friends opposite. We are not responsible for it in any way, but we are doing our best, morning, noon and night, to counteract it. With respect to the pledge of the Prime Minister and the Conservative party made to the people of Canada that a special session of parliament would be called to deal with this all-important and paramount question, that pledge was kept, were it not for the relief granted at the special session of 1930

The Budget-Mr. McDade
this dominion would be in a very poor plight indeed.
Prior to the special session there were no substantial expenditures made in the Mira-michi district, the popular name for the county of Northumberland. It is true there were a handful of men at work in the towns of Chatham, Douglastown, and also a few at Bay du Vin and Burnt Church, but as a result of the measures adopted at the last session, innumerable men have gone to work. A return covering the expenditures for unemployment relief in the county of Northumberland has been tabled in this house. The auditor's general report for the province of New Brunswick has been presented and shows that there was expended in the county of Northumberland alone during 1930 the sum of $600,000, including the amount contributed by the federal administration under the provisions of the Unemployment Relief Act. In addition, there were further public moneys expended to relieve unemployment.
Under the regime of my hon. friends opposite the Canadian National Railways last year issued a circular to the tie contractors in the province of New Brunswick to the effect that no tie contracts would be awarded in the province of New Brunswick during 1930. That state of affairs continued until after the elections but as a result of the good offices of the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Manion) the Canadian National Railways changed their attitude and tie contracts were awarded in the county to the extent of $150,000. In this county there has been expended a total of three-quarters of a million dollars in the relief of unemployment.
While conditions in the county of Northumberland are none too good, they are not alarming. Our basic industry is lumbering, and we all know and appreciate the decline which has occurred in this industry, not only in New Brunswick but elsewhere throughout Canada. I urge that further assistance be granted, and ask my good friend the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Stewart) to deal charitably with the constituency which I have the honour to represent in the event of supplementary estimates being presented to this house.
This government has given Canada a tariff which will protect Canadian industry and give employment to Canadian workmen. The policies adopted by this administration have resulted in the establishment in Canada of some 87 new industries. How my hon. friends opposite would blow the trumpet if in ten short months there had been established, as
a result of their administration, this number of new industries. The increase in the tariff will protect Canadian industries and give employment to Canadian workmen. There will be no increase in the cost of the commodities to the consumer. This was assured at the last special session, and further assurances have been given by the administration in the presentation of this budget. Provision is being made for the imposition of an excise tax in the event of the manufacturer taking undue advantage of the tariff in order to raise the price to the consumer. This is a new departure because under former adminis1-trations an increase in the tariff of necessity meant an increase in the price to the consumer. I am pleased to see that the present adminstration has protected the consumer.
Statistics reveal that during the last ten years Canada imported from the United States goods to the value of $6,754,000,000, ' as opposed to exports to the United States valued at $4,623,000,000, leaving an adverse trade balance for the period of 1921A930 inclusive against Canada and in favour of United States of $2,130,000,000. I submit that there is an urgent need for higher protection for our Canadian industries and our Canadian workmen. During the last ten years while this country has been under the regime of my hon. friends opposite we have lost the enormous amount of $2,130,000,000 which might have gone into the development of Canadian industry and provided additional employment for Canadian workmen. The regime of my hon. friends opposite was characterized by great activity in the wheat industry, but the administration of that day did not give sufficient attention to the study of the great needs of diversity in industry and the equalizing of the balance betwen agriculture and industry. When we realize and appreciate the import of these striking figures, I submit that the only policy which this administration could follow was that policy which the Canadian people endorsed in July last, the Canada first policy enunciated by my right hon. leader (Mr. Bennett).
I congratulate the administration of the day on the action taken to exclude the importation of Russian goods. This is a step calculated to assist our own industries, and the leadership demonstrated by the administration is something which other nations of the world might reasonably emulate. Conditions in Russia have been described by different speakers in this house, and I submit that we do not wish, as a Christian country, to associate in trade relations with a nation that has forgotten God and the principles of Christianity. Moreover, the bringing in of Russian goods, particularly coal, at this time would place this product in competition with our own coal and this would naturally have an injurious effect upon the 'industry of the country, so much so that the wages paid would be lower. And in any event we should not have anything to do with a country which, as I say, has forgotten God and the principles of Christianity, and which has taken advantage of the men., women and children of the country to advance the selfish ends of the Soviet.
With respect to immigration, I wish to congratulate the minister upon the attitude taken in excluding immigrants except under certain well-defined regulations, until conditions improve in this country. We know that the unemployment which has existed in Canada for some time originated under the regime of my hon. friends opposite; yet no steps were taken by that government to alleviate the situation. Immigrants were induced to come here, and I say it was unfair to them because misrepresentations were employed-not by the administration but by the railway systems. It was also unfair to our own labour, at a time when there was unemployment in the country, to bring in people to compete with our own people. We know what the results have been. Yet the administration of my hon. friends opposite went out of power without taking the one bold and 
logical course of cancelling the existing immigration laws. It remained for the government of my right hon. leader (Mr. Bennett) to take that one bold and logical step and adopt the policy that there should be no further emigration from any country whatever except under certain well known regulations. And we know that the regulations that have been adopted will be honoured in the observance and not in the breach, as was characteristic of the conduct of the department in the past in many instances. I have the fullest confidence in the ability and capacity of the hon. gentleman who has been called to the position of Minister of Immigration (Mr. Gordon) and I know that he will see that the regulations are strictly adhered to. I believe it will be time enough to revise those regulations when Canada does offer to immigrants the opportunities which we should like her to extend.
As proof positive of the fact that the immigration regulations are being respected and adhered to, I would point out that the average general decrease in immigration in April, 1931, as compared with April, 1930, was 83 per cent. The decrease in European immigration was 97 per cent, and in the rest, apart from British or American, 95 per cent. British immigration fell off to 81 per cent and that from the United1 States to 44 per cent. Taking the whole calendar year 1930, there was an average decrease of 36 per cent, the figures being: January, 19 per cent; February, 14 per cent; March, 2 per cent; April, 34 per cent; May, 35 per cent; June, 40 per cent; July, 49 per cent; August, 41 per cent; September, 47 per cent; October, 50 per cent; November, 55 per cent; and December, 58 per cent. It will be noted that most of the more substantial decreases took place after the advent of the new administration and the enforcement of the new regulations.
Evidently the province of New Brunswick thought it was time for a change. The province I have the honour to come from voted almost solidly in support of the new administration. Even my hon. friend from Gloucester (Mr. Yeniot), for whom I have the highest personal regard, had the fight of his life. Let me congratulate him most heartily upon having carried the great county of Gloucester by the smallest majority given any candidate in that county in the history of confederation. To use a race track expression, my hon. friend the ex-Postmaster General just got under the wire. Let me tell him, and again in all fairness to him, because we are the best of friends, that the handwriting is on the wall. The hon. gentleman did not make a tremendous success of himself at

The Budget-Mr. Euler
Ottawa. He was in a new environment, a new arena, and one too large indeed for the hon. gentleman. Let me tell him that there is a young man in the county of Gloucester awaiting the opportunity to meet him in the next political campaign, when-I say this to my hon. friend with all due deference-the ex-Postmaster General will be sunk into political oblivion.
My hon. friend the other evening had some reference to make, when the house was in committee of supply, on the estimates of the fisheries department, to the new regulations affecting the fishermen. I thank him for the interest he manifests in the fishermen of the country. But let me assure him that before he raised his voice in protest against the new regulations the members from New Brunswick had made representations to the minister and action was being taken to see that the regulations, in so far as they might impose hardships on the fishermen, would be amended.

We all like my hon. friend, but, as regards what happened in the province of New Brunswick, the fact is that ten representatives of the great Liberal-Conservative party were returned by very substantial majorities-my hon. friend from Victoria-Carleton (Mr. Smith), by the largest majority given any
candidate there since confederation-while my hon. friend opposite, as I have said, just got in under the wire.
There are several other matters which I could discuss, but my time is limited, and I appreciate very much the indulgence of the house. In conclusion, I have the greatest confidence in Canada, with her wealth of natural resources, the products of the sea, the soil, the mines and the forest and our great industrial plants. I look toward the future with a spirit of optimism. I have the utmost confidence in the ability and capacity of the Prime Minister and his colleagues, and I believe Canada, guided by their leadership, will go forward to immeasurable prosperity. I believe the government will tackle our common problems with a grim determination to see them through in order to restore prosperity to Canada and happiness to the various elements that go to make up this country of ours.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure the hon. member for Northumberland (Mr. McDade), who has just taken his seat, will not regard it as discourteous on my part if I do not follow him into the realm of the speech which he has just delivered to the house, except possibly in one particular to which I shall refer in due course. Indeed, my reason for injecting myself into the debate is largely, although not entirely, because of certain statements which were made by the leader of the government (Mr. Bennett) and by the hon. member for Stanstead (Mr. Hackett) with respect to the national railways. Frankly, I have some misgiving because of the fact that while the Prime Minister made a very exhaustive analysis of the financial situation of the country, including the position of the national railways, to my disappointment I could not read into his speech anything that betrayed any friendliness for the national railways. When he was followed by the hon. member for Stanstead in a speech in which that hon. member very definitely placed himself on record as being opposed not only to the practice which was followed in the conduct of the national railways, but also to the principle, that of public ownership, I felt that some of us who are the friends of public ownership as exemplified in the operation of the national railways, should take issue with him on that point and say to him that if he represents the opinion of the government and if what he said indicates that in any sense this is merely the preliminary of a propaganda against the national railways,
The Budget-Mr. Euler

they are playing with fire and will find they will receive the condemnation of the great majority of the Canadian people.
These attacks upon the national railways come periodically, the last one being, I think, some seven or eight years ago, shortly after the amalgamation of the various roads. We had then in the house and sometimes from both sides attacks made upon the national railways and the principle of public ownership. We had also in the papers what was known as the "whisper of death," which whisper itself died a natural death in the atmosphere of prosperity which came to this country. At that time the national railways were losing quite heavily. Some people even said-and I think the observation came from the party which is now on this side of the house but which was then on the other side -that we should sell the road to the Canadian Pacific for the sum of one dollar. As I say, the national railways had been losing a great deal of money, and I want to remind the house that the reason why the railways were taken over was that they had failed under private ownership. Then as now the enemies of public ownership and of the railways advanced that false syllogism, if I may use the term:	The national railways are
losing money; they are operated under public ownership; therefore public ownership must be a failure. Everyone knows the country took over a series of systems of disconnected railways: the old Canadian Northern, the Grand Trunk Pacific, the National Transcontinental, the old Grand Trunk, to which was also joined as a matter of operation the old Intercolonial railway. Everyone knows that these railways-and I shall not include the Intercolonial-had failed absolutely under private ownership. When they were taken over, it became the duty of those who were placed in charge of them to combine and coordinate them into one great railway system. That, and their proper equipment, required the expenditure of enormous sums. I need not say it has been the opinion of the people of Canada and of people outside Canada that great success has been attained in the amalgamation and operation of that system.
Until a year or less than a year ago we heard no complaint with regard to the national railways. The record was one of consistent progress. I think I may say without contradiction that politics were eliminated from the management of those railways; that the service became excellent so that the people of Canada took a pride in the operation of their own system. The deficits were being reduced 
from year to year, so much so that our hon. friends opposite-and I do not know that I blame them particularly for doing so-began to speak of the success of the railways and to claim credit for it. I may mention the Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie) as one who commented on the success that had attended the operation of the national railways. Perhaps they feared, quite naturally, that the King government which was then in office might receive too much credit and make a little political capital out of the success of the system. Therefore they said that the former government should not receive credit for what had been accomplished but rather the Conservative party should have it because they were the ones responsible for initiating the amalgamation of the roads. I do not care which party takes credit for the success of the national railways. There were on both sides men who were ardent supporters of the principle o.f public ownership, just as there were on both sides men who were not so much enamoured of it. Now since the whole world, both railways of Canada and the railways of the United States have fallen upon evil days, the enemies of public ownership, who had remained silent while the road was making such undoubted progress, are out again in full cry. Have they forgotten that the national railways were taken over because private ownership was a failure? Do they not know that in the United States practically every railroad of any importance and many of no great importance had all at some time or another gone into the hands of receivers, and this all under private ownership?
The Prime Minister inferentially and the hon. member for Stanstead very definitely have charged extravagance in the matter of both capital expenditure and maintenance. I have no intention of defending extravagance on the part of anyone, and if it can be conclusively proven that the extravagance is gross, that it seriously impedes the national progress and the progress of the railway itself, I have no defence to make. I have not any doubt that in the operation of an enterprise so stupendous, so enormous as the Canadian National Railways, where they expend each year literally hundreds of millions of dollars, where they operate over 22,000 miles of road, some mistakes have been made. The management of the road is not superhuman; they will make some mistakes, but as far as I have been able to learn, those mistakes have not been of such a serious nature that they should wipe out the undoubted excellence of the management that has been displayed to date.

The Budget-Mr. Euler
One particular branch of the activities of the railway which has been mentioned as an extravagance has been the building of hotels, golf courses and things of that sort. The other day in the railways and shipping committee, Sir Henry Thornton, the president of the road, made an explanation of the moneys expended on those activities. He stated, which I think is true, that the tourist business of Canada is perhaps the second largest industry of the country, that it brings into this country something like $300,000,000 per annum. He made a comparison between the Canadian National Railways and the Canadian Pacific Railway, and he paid all sorts of fine tributes to the Canadian Pacific. He stated that the Canadian Pacific had expended in the last eight years no less a sum than $45,000,000 in building hotels and in the general promotion of the tourist business, as against something like $16,000,000 expended by the Canadian National Railways.
The hon. member for Stanstead made an observation the other day with regard to some $604,000,000 which had been advanced I think almost entirely before the Canadian National Railways as a public-owned system took charge of the various roads comprising the system. He said with reference to this $604,000,000, which is still carried on the books of the nation as an inactive asset and is apparently still recognized by the railway as a sum upon which interest should be charged, that he saw no reason why the interest on that $604,000,000 should not be added to the deficit. I take issue with my hon. friend on that point, for the simple reason that that sum is a legacy from private ownership, and is not chargeable to public ownership at all. I would ask him or anyone else who holds the same opinion, what would have happened if the roads now comprising the national railways had been allowed to go into bankruptcy and had been sold to private interests, at scrap value, no doubt. Does he believe that in that case this country would have had any chance whatsoever of receiving back the $664,000,000 that had been advanced to these roads, or of receiving any securities upon which we could have collected interest? I think that in justice to the principle of public ownership and in justice to ourselves the whole of that $604,000,000 ought to be wiped off the slate because we do not expect to get the money back at any time.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Is the hon. member
aware that a large proportion of that sum, all of it I think with the exception of $157,-
000,000, was advanced after the bankruptcy of the roads but before consolidation?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I know this, that the money that was so advanced, possibly with the exception my hon. friend mentions, was advanced at that time because of the fact that the roads had failed under private ownership, and the reason I am making the statement that it should be written off the books is that when comparison is made, as it is constantly being made, between the Canadian Pacific Railway as a privately owned road-and I have no ill word to say of the Canadian Pacific Railway-and the Canadian National Railways, which' exemplifies the principle of public ownership, it is not fair constantly to charge the publicly owned road with what is really the result of private operation. If we disregard, then, as my hon. friend suggested the other day, the interest on the $604,000,000, which was lost in any case whether we took the roads over or did not take them over, we have I believe an average annual deficit for the last eight years of from $10,000,000 to $14,000,000. There is some difference of opinion as to the amount, but we will say that it is from $10,000,000 to $14,000,000. That is quite a large sum, Mr. Speaker, I admit, but I will say this without any fear of contradiction, that I believe it was well worth it if it was only because of the fact that the people of this country, both through the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Canadian National Railways, had experienced great benefits because of the efficient operation and the service that is being given by these roads. I am not a communist or a socialist, Mr. Speaker, but I am, as I have almost always been, a believer in the principle of public ownership within reasonable limits. I believe in public ownership of those utilities and services upon which depends the prosperity of the mass of the Canadian people, and of services which cannot well be operated by the individual and which in so many cases lend themselves naturally to monopoly. Of such, I think, is the operation of railways. I fear that there are a great many people who condemn public ownership because they do not quite appreciate what the purpose of public ownership really is. To my mind public ownership implies, first of all, service, and service at cost. Private ownership necessarily implies, first, the making of profit, and if good service is given by a privately-owned company like the Canadian Pacific Railway it is primarily done for the purpose
The Budget-Mr. Euler

of securing profits. That is not making any reflection upon private ownership.
I have also heard it stated that we do not want a monopoly in railways. That may be true, but I say this, that the evils of monopoly do not appear in publicly owned utilities as they do in privately owned utilities because of the very fact I stated a moment ago, that the principle upon which private services are operated is the principle of profit. In public ownership monopoly would have no vicious results because the incentive to profit is not present under public ownership.
I have said that the people of this country are proud of the Canadian National Railways, and while the railway for the moment -we do not know how long it may last-has fallen upon evil days, and while we do not like to see a deficit of some $20,000,000 as there was last year, which the Canadian taxpayer to some exent, if not entirely, must pay, should we not remember that the same condition applies relatively to all other railways, and applies not only to railways but to every private business enterprise of almost any kind? And why should we now single out the railways for condemnation of the principle of public ownership because we have a general depression? The railways have had to cope with conditions that have not been faced by other enterprises. I speak now of the competition that is presented by the operation of trucks and automobiles which have cut tremendously into the revenues of the railways. Again, our railways, including the Canadian Pacific Railway, especially during the last year and the year before, have suffered a great diminution in their receipts because the wheat of western Canada was not moving as usual through the ordinary channels.
It is notorious, Mr. Speaker, that a great deal of waste occurs in the operation of the rival lines. I think there is no doubt about that. There is a great deal of duplication, and the inference by some who support private ownership is that the proper solution of the difficulty is the amalgamation of the two roads. I think it was about eight years ago that in this house I had the temerity to make a speech in which I drew attention to the fact that it was pretty well established by what I regarded as the highest authority in the country that as much as $100,000,000 could be saved if the railways of Canada could be merged into one system. I said then that the amalgamation of the two roads might very well be considered in order to eliminate the waste, but that if such a merging did take place it should be Under public ownership, and not under private
EMr. Euler.]
ownership. Some interest was taken in the matter at that time in the .press, but it was not very long before the country became very prosperous, and no more interest was taken in the subject. But I did feel then, as I feel now, that the logic of events and the necessities of the case may still some day force that amalgamation, and when it does come, if it does, I for one would say that it must be under public ownership and not under private ownership. So much for the national railways.
I would like to deal for a few moments with the budget, and I want my hon. friends opposite to believe me when I say that I have no intention of dealing with it from a partisan standpoint but strictly on its merits. The Prime Minister and his government to-day are facing heavier responsibilities than any other government of Canada has faced. They have imposed heavy taxation, I am very certain that even with the taxation that they have imposed there will be an increase in the national debt when the fiscal year has expired.
The government has put a tax of 40 cents a ton on hard coal, in spite of the fact that hard coal is still the fuel used by most of the people in Ontario. Of course, the tax imposed will result in an increase in the price of hard coal. On soft coal the duty has been increased from 50 to 75 cents per ton. Postage has been increased by 50 per cent. The stamp tax, or nuisance tax, which I had hoped would be entirely eliminated, an action which would have met with the approval of every business man in the country, has been amplified. Cheques under $10 because of the new legislation will have to carry the excise stamp. I am sorry the government saw fit to impose that tax. The tariff on automobiles has been increased, and a tariff has been placed on oranges. I may remind hon. members that oranges are no more produced in this country than is hard coal. Now we come to the sales tax. May I add at this time that I am not particularly criticizing all of these items; I admit that something has to be done. However the government has seen fit to increase the sales tax from one per cent to 4 per cent, a tax which falls most heavily upon those who are least able to pay it. Substantial increases have been made in many tariff items. The government may well feel its responsibilities all the more because of the fact-and I think I will not be contradicted by my hon. friends opposite-that they succeed a government which gave efficient administration without a trace of scandal, a government which consistently reduced taxation from year to year, which consistently reduced the national debt

The Budget-Mr. Euler
from year to year, which had a series of surpluses from year to year, which registered trade expansion in foreign countries consequent upon its policies of development of foreign trade, and promoted a prosperity in Canada such as had never before been known.
My hon. friends opposite have the responsibility of dealing with the present situation, which in itself is serious enough, and of carrying out the promises which they made during the election campaign. I have no intention of taking a great deal of time in dealing with the election promises to which reference has been made so often during the present and the last session, yet it is almost impossible fairly to represent the present situation without making some few comments in that regard.
Concerning the promises made I refer particularly to the matter of unemployment. The Prime Minister and his supporters most definitely promised throughout the campaign that they would end unemployment. I say that our friends opposite cannot get away with the excuse that they have not had sufficient time to fulfil their promises, and that they were not going to fulfil them immediately. I appreciate fully the fact that it was not possible for them to end unemployment immediately; they were faced with a world condition and nobody expected them to end it immediately. I say however that willingly or otherwise they allowed the impression to go abroad among the public during the election campaign that they were going to end unemployment at once and that almost immediately every man would have a job. Indeed it has been stated and also denied that some of my hon. friends opposite said unemployment would be ended in the short period of three days. I am not going to attribute that statement to my hon. friend the Minister of Justice, because although it was ascribed to him he has denied the statement. Perhaps if the statement was made it carried the biblical meaning that a thousand years are but as a day. If we accept that meaning, then the government has three thousand years in which to end unemployment, and nobody will be able to say they did not fulfil their promises. I am not one of those who have talked blue ruin; I never have done so because I have a great deal of confidence that Canada will recover. Nevertheless unemployment is a great deal worse to-day than it was at the time of the election. I hope my hon. friends are in a position to do something to remedy unemployment, not merely to relieve those who unfortunately find themselves unemployed. The
820,000,000 which -was voted during the special session did nothing towards a proper solution of the difficulty; it merely brought temporary relief to those who were suffering. Certainly it did not go to the crux of the situation and bring about a condition whereby unemployment would be ended altogether. In connection with the promises made by my hon. friends opposite I make this criticism- and I think it is a fair one-that to the extent to which they owe office to the promises which, they did not or could not carry out, they are reaping where they did not sow. . Certainly however nobody envies them the harvest they are now gathering.
I think it is fair to say that the Prime Minister prescribes the raising of the tariff as the cure-all of our economic troubles. I will admit immediately that the tariff presents a most difficult problem. My hon. friends on this side of the house know that I am not one of those who say that the tariff cannot be used for the promotion of industry. I have never been at any time, however, and I am not now, in favour of an extremely high tariff which extracts undue profits from the consumer, or a tariff which will lead to reprisals on the part of other nations with which we do business, and thus destroy our export business. To my mind the ideal condition, in the world would be one wherein we had no tariffs whatever. I suppose the ideal condition, if we could have it, would be an entire absence of international barriers, a condition under which industries would thrive in the places best adapted to their operation, as near as possible to their markets, to water power, population, and efficient and economic means of transporting the necessary raw materials. That condition, however, is not possible. The matter which troubles me particularly is that while theoretically every man must be a free trader, how are we going to be free traders in a protectionist world all the countries of which are from year to year raising higher customs barriers? We must all admit, however, that the principle applies that if we do not buy goods from other countries we cannot sell to them.
I should like to point out a rather peculiar condition which came to my notice the other day. We know there were some fairly drastic upward revisions of the tariff at the special session of parliament, particularly as applied to commodities coming from the United States. I find that while our entire imports decreased about 30 per cent since the last special session, the importations from the United States of dutiable goods decreased
The Budget-Mr. Euler

32-8 per cent and the importations of free goods decreased 34-4 per cent. I am not going to place any interpretation upon those figures, although the apparent conclusion would be that the trade depression had more to do with the reduction of importations to this country than the tariff which was passed at the last session.
During the presentation of his budget address the Prime Minister read a list of 87 industries which since the special session had begun operations in Canada. Among those mentioned was the Aero Corporation of Canada situated at Kitchener, Ontario. As that is the city from which I come I have tried to find the location of that factory. I am afraid however that the industry has been very well named-it is entirely up in the air. I can find no trace - of it-only rumour. I hope the other industries my hon. friend has mentioned are more substantial than the one mentioned as having been established in the city of Kitchener.
Hon. members know I have always believed in a reasonable or moderate degree of protection. In fact, I agree with the words of the Prime Minister himself when he described a tariff which would permit of competition. I would like hon. members to observe particularly the word "competition." Throughout the last election campaign the Prime Minister on many platforms in the country advocated a tariff which would admit of competition and equal opportunity for producers within our own country. I do not think any hon. member could find a great deal of fault with such a tariff. In fact I might go a little further and say I would be a little bit inclined to favour the Canadian producer over the foreign manufacturer.
