speechtext:
That taxes shall be gathered in the money marts of the country and that the ultimate consumer must bear the burden are the two axioms in direct taxation. But that taxes shall become retroactive is a dangerous policy, and would tend to demoralize the financial stability of the country's industries.
The weakness of the Prime Minister's budget as presented to the house yesterday is his confession that he has not yet finished the most important measure of tariff adjustment, a delay which has been injurious to that stability and confidence necessary to inspire the investors who may be considering ^constructive advances.
That it has been an herculean task for the chief executive can be readily granted, but the country looks to the premier to overcome his task by securing competent help and expert advisers. No one man can handle the multifarious problems of finance, no matter how talented he may be.

The Budget-Mr. Howard
I do not think any hon. member has any doubt as to which side of politics the Ottawa Journal is on. The day after the budget was presented it stated in headlines: "Bennett budget increases taxes. Puts duty on hard coal and one cent tax on letters." I think it is generally conceded that throughout the length and breadth of this country even the subsidized press of my hon. friends opposite has not been enthusiastic about this budget.
Considerable credit has been given to the Minister of Finance for the wonderful success of the conversion loan. May I state that I marvel not that the conversion loan was oversubscribed but that it was not subscribed for to the extent of one billion dollars within three days after the announcement. I believe what success this loan attained has been due to the publicity carried on in the newspapers. Does the house realize the psychological state of the citizens of Canada just previous to the launching of this loan? Every hon. member knows that the monthly letters usually issued by stockbrokers always state that things are going to be better, but on June 1 the investment firm of Craig, Luther and Irvine issued a letter containing the following:
Industrial production and general business have as yet shown no sign of definite improvement. Foreign trade returns for April were at the lowest point for that month in any year since 1922, output of iron and steel, after making some recovery earlier in the year, is again tending downward. Weakness of commodity prices persists, and the conduct of world trade already hampered by tariff barriers is restricted still further by depreciation of many foreign exchanges.
The report continues:
Over-capitalization is not confined to the newsprint companies-
And again:
There is a danger, too, that the wage scale controversy, already looming large in the public mind, may cause acute unsettlement before the final phase of the depression is reached.
For the last two months stock market prices have been falling from five to ten points per day. Bank stock prices are fallingj and bond prices have been at their lowest point for years in Canada. There had been created in the minds of the people of Canada a feeling where even the small investor was on the verge of going to the savings bank to with- . draw his deposits and bring them back home to bury in the cellar. The people had got to the stage where they did not know what was going to happen and the only thing in which they had confidence was the future of Canada, and therefore they felt the only thing they could do was to renew their notes. Far
from being a success, the mental attitude of the people being what it is, I believe the conversion loan has been a failure.
I do not wish to repeat the prices and statistics which I gave in a previous debate this year, but I hold in my hand a copy of La Tribune of Sherbrooke under date of June 6, in which some figures are given to which I wish to refer. This is most important, because only twice since confederation has the population of Sherbrooke, which has been constantly increasing, decreased. These two occasions were in 1919 and this last year. The census was completed on Saturday, June 6, which was last Saturday, and we find that in spite of the fact that there were in Sherbrooke during the past year 432 births, there was a shrinkage of population from 28,757 to 28,698. I cite these figures just to show what is going on.
Two months ago in this house I quoted prices and we mavelled at the low prices of dairy products, including butter, which I quoted at that time at 28 and 30 cents. Since then the price has dropped to 19 and 20 cents. This last week the creameries paid the farmers 21 cents a pound on butter fat which, on a 3i per cent basis, means 731 cents per 100 pounds for their milk.
I do not want anyone to think for one moment that I am a socialist, nor that I have communistic tendencies. I believe that the Canadian capitalistic system is the best of any so far. I do say, however, that in periods of extraordinary depression, such as we are going through now, the rich people should be made to pay and not the poor. When times improve and the common people are in a better position to pay taxes, then I shall be perfectly satisfied and I shall be one of the first to give consideration to capital and also to wealth. But at the present time I submit that the Prime Minister had no right to increase taxation on people who cannot afford to pay it. Right Hon. Philip Snowden presented his budget in England juat a few days ago and one of the outstanding clauses in it was this: "No increase in taxation." I am sure that no one will argue that Canada is as badly off as England; yet Mr. Snowden has declared at this time that there shall be no increase in taxation in the old country.
The city of Sherbrooke, in their small way, decided this year that they would not have revenue enough to balance their budget without increasing the tax rate at least 2 mills on the dollar, and when they considered the proposition this is the conclusion they arrived at:	After examining the accounts of the
The Budget-Mr. Howard

proprietors, and knowing the amount of arrears in taxation and the condition of the people, who could not afford to pay more taxes, they decided to allow the deficit to accumulate during this year and possibly next year, and when things are more rosy they will put on taxes to meet their budget.
The other day a man seventy-two years of age left the town of Magog at three o'clock in the morning and walked to a certain construction job twelve miles distant. He arrived before work had begun and was ordered on a new job which was starting. He started at seven o'clock with pick and shovel and worked until one o'clock without a single mouthful of food, for the simple reason that he was so anxious to secure a chance of earning something after having been so long out of work. He came from the county of my hon. friend from Stanstead.
I was out the other day on the site of a job where certain construction work was being carried on, and there I saw twenty-two men standing on either side of the roadway, watching for an opportunity, in the event of anything happening to one of the fellows working there, in order that they might jump in and take his place so as to get a few days work.
Remember, Mr. Speaker, I believe that the country should be run exactly like a private corporation. Is there a single man in this house who, if he had been in business eight years and had had a surplus every year for seven years of that period, when he came to an off year with a deficit, would lock the store, close up the whole thing and quit business? Would he do that, or would he draw on the surpluses he had accumulated in the prosperous years and carry on for the period of depression? While the Liberal government was in power, from 1922 to 1930, they paid off the debt of the country to the extent of $270,000,000; and I claim that, under present conditions, what this government should have done, if they had the interests of the people at heart, was to carry on this year and next year without increasing taxation.
Possibly one should not criticize, but I think it is proper to criticize in this instance. On page 2162 of Hansard the Minister of Finance is reported:
New Industries Established in Canada
Since August, 1930, there has been a marked influx of new concerns from outside countries into the dominion.
I want hon. members to note that. Mind you, this is the Minister of Finance of Canada standing on the floor of the House of 
Commons, knowing that everyone in Canada is paying attention, to his words, and saying that there has been a marked influx
of new industries into Canada. He mentions a lot of these industries. I am not going to go into very many of them, but I will cite five or six examples and leave it to the country to judge whether the right hon. gentleman's observation is a statement even fairly true to fact. As regards Granby, Quebec, the Minister of Finance referred to the Steadfast Rubber Company, Esmond Mills, Limited, of Canada, and the A.B.C. Washer Company. These are all beginnings of good industries. But every one of them had decided to come to Canada before it was ever dreamed that there would be a change of administration. The right hon. gentleman also referred to Henry Hamer & Sons Limited, St, George de Beauce, Quebec: a wonderful thing that this company had come to Canada! Mind you, the right hon. gentleman declares that there has been a marked influx of new industries. Do you know what happened in that case? The company was founded five years ago by an hon. gentleman sitting in this house, who put $250,000 into it. And then an English concern came over, because it had got to such a stage that the company could hardly keep things going. They were employing 200 hands, and that English concern saw a chance of taking over the concern at below cost. But it was in operation, and had been there five years. Mr. Edouard Lacroix, M.P., is still president.
The Minister of Finance also referred to, Wooden ware and Toys Limited in Coaticook, in Stanstead county. Now, Mr. Speaker, when I was a member of the industrial committee of the Sherbrooke board of trade, we invited the company to come to Sherbrooke and we entertained them. As a matter of fact, we could not find a kind of building suitable to them and the result was that they delayed and delayed until finally they found exactly the sort of building they wanted and purchased it. But they had decided two years before to come. Then as to Sherbrooke. The Minister of Finance looking across the floor of the house at my desk, and shaking his finger, referred to the Teaberry Chewing Gum Company as one of the new industries. The contract was signed on the 15th day of April 1930, and I can assure the house that this industry is not an American concern, as has been suggested. Its establishment is due entirely to the initiative of two energetic young men, Mr. Leopold Chevalier and Georges Henri Denault, who got $30,000 subscribed amongst their friends and started the

The Budget-Mr. Howard
business. And when they began they did not dream that the government would change.
I could go further, taking example after example to prove the inaccuracy of the list. The right hon. member intimated that there were some eighty-seven industries established within the ten months of this administration. Allowing the same ratio for the next two months, this would mean that there have come into Canada, under this administration, in its first twelve months of office, one hundred and four new industries. He did not make any discount for failures and people who had gone out of business during the period. Let us give them credit for the whole 104, and we are told that this was a "marked influx of new industries." But do hon. members know how many industries came to Canada in 1930 and how many in 1929, during the administration of the present leader of the opposition? Mind you, 104 under the present administration meant "a marked influx," but in 1930 there came into Canada 652 industries and in 1929 there came into Canada 759 industries.

speechtext:
on grain grown in western Canada than does the man in Denmark, Germany or England, who is feeding bacon hogs; moreover, he can take his bacon across the channel in a small boat whereas our product has to be shipped in high-priced vessels, at high freights. On top of that comes this duty of 25 cents a bushel against corn. I am not going to criticize that duty if it is properly administered; but if you read the tariff schedules carefully you will find in them the most extraordinary thing that I have ever seen since I have examined Canadian budgets. If a farmer uses Argentine or any American corn to feed hogs or cows for fattening purposes in connection with the dairy industry of Canada, he pays 25 cents a bushel on it, but if he happens to be one of the millionaire cereal manufacturers, making 200 per cent profit even in this time of depression, he does not pay one cent of duty on his corn.
On top of that, there is the, four per cent sales tax. Let me give an instance to show how this will be applied. A returned soldier and his wife were living in Foster, in the constituency of my hon. friend from Brome-Missisquoi (Mr. Pickel). This man had made arrangements with the soldier settlement board, to whom he was a debtor, under which during these hard times he would pay over one-half of his earnings each month to them and the other half to his grocer. In the first half of the month of April his earnings were $4.70. He gave $2.35 to the SoldieT Settlement Board, and $2.35 to his grocer. During the last half of April you might say that things were looking up for him for he got $9.50 for his services, and he gave $4.75 to the Soldier Settlement Board and $4.75 to his grocer. Now the government want him to pay 4 per cent sales tax in addition, while at the same time they say to the man whose income is over $1,000,000 a year, and there are twenty-five of them in Canada: We are going to refund you $117,000 annually and stick this other poor fellow for the 4 per cent sales tax.
Everybody in Canada had expected that this budget would do away with the dumping legislation that was passed at the last session, and that after the government had had time to study the matter it would bring down a real Canadian budget. But there is no sign of that cancellation in this budget. Let me give another illustration. Last week a boy employed in a garage in Lennoxville, working ten hours a day amongst the grease and oil for $2.50, decided that the only way in which he could get advancement was by getting a better education. He could not go to school, and there did not happen to be any night 
school in Lennoxville, even though the provincial government is pretty good to us, so he subscribed to a course in aeroplane engine mechanics with the International Correspondence School, costing $75. He was going to put in his spare time studying. Everybody is familiar with the examination papers and books that that school sends out. This boy working in a garage had ambition enough to want to improve his mind in order to 'better his position in life, and what do you think the collector of customs in Sherbrooke charged him for duty when his first books arrived? They asked him to pay $28 in duty. He could not afford it, so he had to forego the chance of a better education.
Once before this session I have put on Hansard the case of a man who imported fruit trees. I expected to see in this budget a provision for the removal of the famous dump duty on fruit trees. This man came to Ottawa, and finally after borrowing money from his friends and securing endorsements he paid the duty so that he could release the trees. In order to get his trees, instead of paying a duty of $644.28, he had to pay $3,472.18. That was absolutely unfair. There is not a single Canadian who will say that it was fair, and I say to this government that unless that is rectified and justice is done to this man, they will not get a single seat in the next election in the eastern townships.
Then there is the three cents postage, and the tax on tea, and the coal taxes. Poor old Quebec has not any coal mines, and our people have to buy coal. Our neighbour across the line has coal to sell. Personally I burn 200 tons of Sydney slack coal per year, but that has nothing to do with the question. Anthracite coal is used by the small householder in our province for heating purposes, and it must be used.

maintopic: THE NEW TARIFF AND THE HEAVIER TAXATION
speechtext:
Anthracite has to be used by the small householder for heating purposes, and the average householder during the winter season will have to burn six to eight tons of hard coal. This forty cents a ton duty will mean that the dealer will raise the price at least one dollar per ton, which means that the average householder will have to pay from six to eight dollars more for his coal during the winter, or -from $1.50 to $2 a month more. That is a tax that is put on the poor people, while at the same time the government relieves the rich man with an income of $1,000,000 from paying $117,000, although he can well afford to pay it.

The Budget-Mr. Howard
I come to the insurance tax. The government is going to tax insurance premiums. Evidently the Minister of Finance was not very well posted on that legislation. Does he know one of the reasons why insurance rates are higher in Canada than they should 'be? It is because American companies, capitalized at fifty or a hundred million dollars, come into our small towns and if they cannot get one good risk they walk out, but if they can get one or two or three or five dandy risks, they take them at practically no rate at all, and in order to get even the Canadian companies have to charge higher rates because the best risks are gone. What does this proposal mean, to put a 15 per cent tax on insurance premiums of companies not licensed to do business in Canada? It will not help Canadian insurance companies one five cent piece. It will simply mean that the Canadian who is getting a little better rate will have to pay that extra tax out of his own pocket.
Now I come to one of the most extraordinary examples of budget taxation that I have ever heard of. I refer to the magazine tax. I shall not quote the exact words of the Minister of Finance, but hon. gentlemen all remember how in making his budget speech he said that he went to a newsstand and there saw 350 magazines, and most of them were not fit for Canadians to read. With that I agree, but why not do what the late Hon. George Boivin did when he was Minister of Customs, bar them entirely? Putting a tax on these magazines will not keep them out, and it will not be the American publishers that will pay the tax, but the boy right here at home will have to pay it because he is one of those fellows who is trying to improve his mind.

maintopic: THE NEW TARIFF AND THE HEAVIER TAXATION
speechtext: On Snappy Stories?

maintopic: THE NEW TARIFF AND THE HEAVIER TAXATION
speechtext:
I am a subscriber to the
Canadian Geographic Magazine, and only yesterday I received my form for renewal, and on it was printed that the subscription in Canada was S3, S3.50 in the United States and 84 for all other countries. I leave it to the house to judge who is going to pay the tax. The same applies to American magazines coming into Canada. The man who reads the magazine is going to pay the tax. This magazine tax will not make a particle of difference in the matter of keeping out literature that you do not want Canadians to read.
Then there is the new automobile tax. If there is one industry in Canada which for years has taken the last dollar out of the Canadian people, it is the automobile industry, and I say that the automobile tax brought down in this budget is one of the
most criminal pieces of legislation. The finance minister stood on the floor of this house and said that the tax on the cheap cars was not changed. That was calculated to give the impression to the Canadian people that the finance minister was helping the common people of this country, but everybody knows that since the famous short .session last September the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Rj'ckman) has applied the dumping legislation to automobiles.
Then there is the corporation tax. In case the government would not get the money in quick enough, after the companies had made their returns, filed their incomes and paid their taxes, the government say: We want seven or eight million dollars quickly, and so we will make that legislation retroactive. That means that the corporations will have to pay the tax after they have paid out their dividends to the shareholders. That is absolutely terrible legislation, and there is no question that the country will say so.
Then there is the excise tax of one per cent. That is not added to the sales tax but is imposed on every single thing that comes into Canada no matter what it is, and even if it is on the free list. The cotton manufacturers, for instance, will have to pay one per cent on their raw material coming into Canada, and the silk manufacturers in Canada will have to pay that tax on their raw material coming in from Japan, although that Canadian industry employs the second highest paid labour in the world, and some of their product is even being sold in countries adjacent to where they got the raw silk. Yet one per cent excise tax is imposed on their raw material-and as well there is the four per cent sales tax, the stamp tax, the tea tax, and all the rest of them. I do not know just in what position the common people are going to find themselves.
I come to the question of old age pensions. Many people say: Well, at least the Prime Minister has fulfilled part of his promise. Let me say that if the Prime Minister of Canada had consulted the finance minister of Canada, and told him of the promises he had made to the people and that Quebec had swallowed the bait that the federal government was going to bear 100 per cent of the cost of old age pensions-had he done that, the old people in the province of Quebec would have received their pensions. But because the government is going to bear only 75 per cent of the cost, do you know how that will work out, Mr. Speaker? The people of the province of Quebec at the present time,

The Budget-Mr. Howard

through their institutions, both Roman Catholic and English Protestant-and I believe they are the finest and best in any part of Canada-are at present putting their hand in one of their pockets and taking care of their own poor. Under this legislation they put their hand in the other pocket and hand their money to the federal treasury to take care of the poor in the other fellow's province.
I wish to say a few words about the tariff board. It is scarcely necessary to say anything on that subject, because I think nearly all the people in Canada will admit that when the Prime Minister disbanded the tariff advisory board, he made the greatest mistake of his political career. Now he proposes to put on the statute books of Canada legislation to provide that the members of a proposed new board will be appointed for ten years. With the knowledge that the present government will go out of office in three years at the outside, the Prime Minister is trying to have formed a tariff board which will dictate the policies when the Liberal government assumes office. I do not think the people of Canada will stand for such legislation and I hope it will be withdrawn.

maintopic: THE NEW TARIFF AND THE HEAVIER TAXATION
speechtext: In closing may I say that I have decided that the present Minister of Finance has lost touch with the common people.

maintopic: THE NEW TARIFF AND THE HEAVIER TAXATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it has been indeed refreshing and illuminating to hear the speech by the hon. member for Sherbrooke (Mr. Howard). I cannot say that his remarks have been particularly convincing. He has disclosed some new facts, however, for which we should probably be thankful. For one thing, he told us that the savings banks of Canada are in such a precarious condition that people are considering the withdrawal of their funds. To be honest, I have not heard of such a condition. He also told us that books which were coming into Canada and which could be used for the technical education of young men in his district are being taxed. I should suggest to him that he have a close conversation with his right hon. leader and try to convince the right hon. gentleman to change his attitude toward technical education. The young men to whom the hon. member for Sherbrooke referred would then be able to work through the day and study at night. Up to the present time the right hon. leader of

the opposition has been consistent only in opposing further advances for technical education.
The hon. member for Sherbrooke made further statements regarding firms beginning operations in Canada, but I think when he gave the number he should have given the names. My hon, friend has been guilty, as have many other hon. members in the house, of making statements which although supposed to be founded on facts were not properly proven. In these days when people read newspapers they accept as true the information contained therein. If these firms had begun operations in Canada would not the Liberal party have used that fact for campaign propaganda? Last summer they were searching for anything they could lay their hands on to save themselves before the electors of Canada. It was an open secret in the minds of Canadians that from the day the campaign opened the late Prime Minister of this dominion was on the defensive. At no time during the campaign did he change his position to that of the offensive, and his record was reflected in his defeat. In the history of Canada has there ever been a party so disappointed in defeat, and a party so completely unable to hide that fact from the public. I knew the right hon. leader of the opposition when he was Prime Minister of Canada; I had hoped that as leader of the opposition he would be equally as efficient. The manner in which the official opposition has been operating in this house during the present session, however, is not a credit to Canada. While the Prime Minister is responsible for the conduct of the house he is not responsible for the conduct of the followers of the leader of the opposition. As I go through the speeches of my right hon. friend and those of his followers I find that at least to the extent of two-thirds they are made up of newspaper clippings. Thank God there are newspapers published in Canada or the Liberal party would be wanting in campaign speeches and also speeches by Liberal members in the House of Commons.
At least on fourteen different occasions the right hon. leader of the opposition in his speech referred to the method of approach of the Prime Minister of Canada. The right hon. leader of the opposition does not yet realize that he had nine years to demonstrate his method of approach and that the people of Canada decided on July 28 last that his method of approach was no longer required. The right hon. leader of the opposition, speaking of spiritual things, said that the method of approach adopted by the present Prime

The Budget-Mr. Plunkett
Minister was not correct and the tendency created was one of dissension. May I remind the right hon. gentleman that he had nine years to demonstrate the right spirit and the proper method of approaching all the problems of Canada. What did that nine years cost the citizens of Canada? It compelled the population of 10,000,000 people in Canada in the years 1928 and 1929 to buy from the United States goods valued at $1,719,237,031. In the same period a population of 120,000,000 people bought from us goods valued at $1,014,644,064 leaving a trade balance in favour of our good neighbours to the south of $704,592,967. Those figures demonstrate what the method of approach adopted by the present leader of the opposition cost the people of Canada in the two years I have mentioned. It further cost them a loss in population of 132,619 persons. "Method of approach"-does the leader of the opposition consider his is the only method in the world, that he sets the whj's and wherefores of good procedure simply because he has written a book entitled "Industry and Humanity"?
Now let us see what is the opinion of two of the leading American newspapers in regard to the tariff proposals of this government. It was said by the right hon. leader of the opposition when he was Prime Minister that under no consideration must we do anything to provoke the United States. He really meant that we must not do anything to hurt their feelings. Here is the comment of the Washington Post on the budget.
Premier Bennett does not intend to let Canadians remain idle while they are supplied with the necessities of Life from other countries, if he can avoid it.
The objective is to reserve the home market for domestic producers, letting foreigners contribute what Canada cannot well produce for herself.
The New York Times says:
Here is a friendly nation, our neighbour across the street, our best customer. We have shut the door in his face. Now he is going to do a little door-shutting himself. Such is the sinful nature of man. When there are door-openers enough in Washington, there will be plenty of them in Ottawa.
I am thankful, Mr. Speaker, that the present government is determined to uphold the dignity of this country and to maintain the self-respect of our people.
The late Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) stated recently in this house:
The government is the by-produot of financial depression. My hon. friends opposite are its offspring.
Now, who are responsible for this depression? Who caused this "offspring" to be born? The history of Canada shows that when in trouble her people have always turned to the Conservative party. In their extremity last year they were compelled to use this "by-product," and put their trust in the Conservative party-a party which has never failed the country in times of crisis. The late Minister of Justice concluded his remarks in these words:
I will finish that speech somewhere, sometime.
Just an exhibition of the bitterness of disappointment. He could not realize that he was on the opposition benches. If the hon. member will come to Victoria I shall be happy to welcome him and he will be at liberty to speak as long as he wishes. The right hon. leader of the opposition was out there last year and spoke for three hours. The people listened attentively and then voted against his candidate. I assure him that he will have a warm welcome should he come again. The former Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) in the course of a speech delivered recently in this house said:
We are being asked what we would do. I do not think that is a fair question, but I intend to accept it as one. In the past no opposition leader or opposition that I know of has ever produced a policy for the gsvernmemt, nor should they be expected to.
When Mr. Mackenzie was in power in 1877, the Conservative opposition under the right hon. Sir John A. Macdonald brought forward their policy of protection-the national policy -and in the ensuing election they were swept into office and remained there for several years. When eventually the Liberal party secured power they lived off that fiscal policy and never created a new one. What was the history of that party while in opposition to Sir John A. Macdonald's government? They put forward several fiscal policies under various names, such as "commercial union," "unrestricted reciprocity," "free trade." They were beaten on every one of them, and at last in 1911 under their famous leader, the late Sir Wilfrid Laurier, they presented to the country their policy of reciprocity with the United States, but the electorate most decisively refused to accept it. What happened on July 28 last? Countervailing duties were advocated by my hon. friends opposite and introduced by the Hon. Charles Dunning, but we have never heard of that policy since. Where has the Prince of Saskatchewan gone? Has he been replaced by the Prince of Nova Scotia as the financial critic of the govern-

ment? The Prince of Saskatchewan was the author of the countervailing duties.

The hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Mackenzie) speaking on the address in reply to the speech from the throne is reported at page 362 of Hansard as follows:
The tariff policies of this government last September had built ramparts of ruin around the dominion, and exhausted all the consuming and purchasing powers of the Canadian workmen.
Perhaps he had read one of the Right Hon. Arthur Meighen's speeches; I do not know. The absurdity of such a statement is demonstrated by the success of the conversion loan last week, when subscriptions of $639,000,000 were received from the people of Canada. Does that look like the "ramparts of ruin"? Another conclusive answer to such idle talk is to be found in the establishment of 87 new factories and the steadily increasing number of men who are returning to work. It would appear to me that some of the statements made in this house are due to lack of thought. At the conclusion of his address in criticism of the budget the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth (Mr. Ralston) moved an amendment the concluding clauses of which are:
That the existing economic depression can only be overcome by policies which are of a character,
(a)	to relieve unemployment-
Now, Mr. Speaker, since the legislation passed at the special session last September there has been spent on unemployment $69,690,948, which resulted in 248,000 people being relieved. The hon. gentleman did not tell us what he would do under the circumstances. The policies of his party are always up in the clouds; they are always stated so indefinitely as to allow an opening for retreat if party exigencies render retreat desirable.
(b)	to restore to a condition of parity the relation between the purchasing powers of all classes-
No hon. member seems to want to have anything to say about that statement, and I am sure I do not. It might be well to ask the right hon. leader of the opposition to elucidate this somewhat ambiguous
IMr. Plunkett.]
language; he may be able to disclose its true meaning.
(c) to bring about more equitable distribution of the burdens of taxation-
A great deal has been said about this being a rich man's budget. Let us see if that is so. First of all there is the increased contribution to old age pensions. As a result of that action by the government I would not be surprised if the provinces in the east now enacted legislation to take advantage of the greater federal assistance, and perhaps the government of Quebec will also take the same course. Surely that tends to equalize the burden of taxation all over the dominion, because, for instance, so far the Quebec government has not seen fit to give its people the benefit of old age pensions. Is increasing the taxation from 8 to 10 per cent on corporations and joint stock companies a poor man's budget? Surely the increase of one cent on letters except those for local delivery tends to equalize the distribution of taxation. How many letters does a poor man write as compared with the extensive correspondence of business men and corporations?
In my opinion the finest feature of this budget is the addition to the postal rates. That gives a fair distribution of taxation. The people are receiving good service and I hope the government will protect the post office by not 'being too far-reaching in its endeavours to establish air service. The present method for the transportation of mail provides much employment; an aeroplane employs only one man where there may be ten employed by the present method.
The stamp tax on cheques is equitable. How many cheques does the poor man make out compared with the rich man? It is not necessary to labour this point, I need only to mention it.
I think the increase in the sales tax from one to four per cent is very equitable, and in this regard we have the precedent set up by the old government who raised it to six per cent. If it was good for them to raise it to six per cent, surely it is good for this government to raise it to four per cent.
Hon. members have been criticizing the banks of this country. I know of no banking system in the world equal to the Canadian. Banks are continually failing in the United States, and yet the other day an attack on our banking system was made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth). Only this evening the hon.

Questions
member for Sherbrooke (Mr. Howard) stated that the people of this country were considering taking their savings out of the banks which they had begun to distrust.
I hope that at the next session of parliament the order paper will not be filled with the useless questions we have been faced with this year. By that time the opposition should be satisfied with their position. They will have realized that they will be in opposition for some years and that they can give as good if not better service in that position than they gave when occupying the benches on this side of the house.
